articles.title_orig: China Leads Green Shipping Corridor Growth but Commercial Progress Remains Limited
articles.title_zh: China Leads Green Shipping Corridor Growth but Commercial Progress Remains Limited
articles.content_orig:
China has become a prominent force in the worldwide push for green shipping corridors, with no fewer than 21 projects connected to the nation, according to a fresh Global Maritime Forum report. The analysis, presented at the group’s yearly gathering in Shanghai, reveals that China represents close to one-fifth of all such initiatives globally and introduced ten additional ventures during 2025.
Read also: Shipping Faces New Compliance Test as Maritime Rules Tighten
Even so, many of these efforts are at an early point. Among the 21 projects tracked as of the end of June this year, a dozen were still being initiated, five were assessing feasibility, three had moved into preparation, and merely one had reached the realisation stage. The furthest along is the Australia-East Asia Iron Ore corridor, which entails running ammonia-fuelled bulk carriers linking Australia’s Pilbara area with China.
The report further observes that a large portion of tomorrow’s marine fuel supply is increasingly centred on China. The nation holds approximately 80% of worldwide green methanol output capacity that has cleared final investment decision, along with over 40% of equivalent green ammonia capacity. Chinese developments in the pipeline aim for yearly output of 30 million tonnes of green methanol and 15 million tonnes of green ammonia by the early 2030s, though the report warns that not every announced project will secure investment.
Bunkering facilities are progressing too. Over ten Chinese ports have set up or are building methanol bunkering capacity, with volumes hitting 100,000 tonnes by mid-2026, compared with 64,000 tonnes across the whole of 2025. Shanghai generates roughly 90% of that total.
Notwithstanding these strides, the financial picture stays tough. Green methanol and ammonia continue to be priced at two to three times conventional marine fuels, even given China’s low production costs, the report found. Battery-electric cargo ships are likewise about double the expense of standard vessels.
Demand is a further barrier. Studies referenced by the Global Maritime Forum indicate that although 65% of cargo owners would pay extra for low-carbon shipping, the typical premium they will accept stands at only 3%.
The report urges more funding for bunkering and fuel distribution networks, tighter harmonisation of Chinese and global fuel certification rules, and policy steps to shrink the price differential.
These conclusions arrive as China starts converting some green shipping ambitions into commercial activity. Earlier this month, the 210,000 dwt newcastlemax Mineral Europa, owned by CMB.TECH and chartered to Australian miner Fortescue, became the first ammonia-powered dry bulk carrier to undertake a commercial voyage. The ship later loaded 1,000 tonnes of green ammonia at Zhoushan in the first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of the fuel worldwide.
In September, China also launched the International Green Shipping Corridor Alliance, uniting 45 companies and organisations from 12 nations to coordinate efforts on alternative fuels, green vessels and port infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.title_zh: Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
articles.content_orig:
As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

articles.title_orig: Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up
articles.title_zh: Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up
articles.content_orig:
Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the riots’ chief instigator and leader of the far-left La France Insoumise (LFI), is currently ranked second in most presidential polls. Marine Le Pen remains the favourite despite her continuing legal problems.
But the polls do not reveal Mélenchon’s strategy, his organisation, his coherence or his ruthlessness. It has become fashionable to dismiss his chances. He is too radical, they say, too inflammatory. As if that has not benefited other modern underdogs.
Born in Tangier in 1951, the former socialist schoolteacher became a senator at 35 and briefly served as a minister under the former PM Lionel Jospin. Mélenchon has spent the past 18 years building a party in his own image. This is his fourth presidential run, and there has been steady progress: in 2022 he came within a point and a half of the second round.
Mélenchon is quite obviously brilliant. Contrary to most other French politicians, who have the literacy of dried oysters, he is well-read and can speak well. He can cite Victor Hugo, whose parliamentary speeches he reveres as much as Les Misérables , as well as Robespierre and Michelet’s history of the Revolution. He is what the French call a tribun , a tribune, an orator, who regularly summons countless minions. His rally in June in Saint-Denis united tens of thousands of people.
Mélenchon has built a formidable political machine. It is hierarchical and motivated, possibly more so than any other party’s. In France, the trained ear can spot when his circle has held one of its internal strategy meetings: rumours start spreading, all using the same turns of phrase.
His team has adapted old-school Red methods to the modern world. Woe betide the victim of their online legions, who will barrage you with threats and insults for days. I was turned into a target after I allegedly argued for the expulsion of Algerian diplomats and the burning of their Paris embassy, following the incarceration of the writer Boualem Sansal.
Mélenchon’s lieutenants owe him every-thing and are quite ready to die for him. They are his Red Guard. First among equals is Manuel Bompard – doctor of applied mathematics, campaign director in 2017 and 2022, elected to his boss’s old seat in Marseille. He is the brains. Next comes Mathilde Panot. An international relations graduate from Sciences Po university, and now president of the parliamentary group, she is the enforcer, a woman who could credibly pass as a territorial and domineering 14th-century tavern keeper. Then there is Sophia Chik-irou, communications director and almost certainly in a relationship with Mélenchon (the leader of the Communist party has called LFI a sect under the spell of a couple).
Add to that the lower rungs, peopled with creatures of marsupial intelligence: National Assembly member Sébastien Delogu, the barely literate Marseille taxi driver whose only qualification is his cab licence; European Parliament member Rima Hassan, born in a Syrian refugee camp and turned ambassador to Gaza, who went on trial this week for glorifying terrorism; Raphaël Arnault, also in the National Assembly, who sits on a state security watchlist and co-founded the Jeune Garde. This is the outfit whose militants are under investigation for the death of 23-year-old Quentin Deranque, bludgeoned to oblivion in a Lyon street in February. Two of those charged with involvement were Arnault’s own parliamentary assistants.
Mélenchon has purged the party of any-one who isn’t deathly loyal. A number of old-timers, some of whom co-founded LFI with him, were ruthlessly cast out and blacklisted after an attempted modern leftist version of a marshals’ mutiny just before the snap election of 2024. The rebels told Mélenchon he was too tainted to be the party’s presidential nominee and should step aside. Five days later, most had official LFI candidates running against them, and their names were no longer mentioned by many former colleagues.
The rebels included my friend Alexis Corbière, an old companion of Mélenchon’s, who, despite the purge, managed to hold on to his seat in the Assembly. His experience featured prominently in a book on the brutality of LFI’s Stalinist tactics, entitled La Meute (‘The Pack’), which enjoyed considerable commercial success.
These lovely characters built LFI’s think-tank: the Institut la Boétie, founded in October 2019 by Bernard Pignerol, a councillor of state and an old friend of the boss. (Étienne de La Boétie wrote Discourse on Voluntary Servitude , a 16th-century essay explaining why whole peoples consent to serve one man…) It’s a facility with impressive political output – a stream of graduates from ten-weekend courses – financed by a million-euro grant from the party and tax-deductible donations which have been referred to the Treasury for scrutiny.
Woe betide the victim of their online legions, who will barrage you with threats and insults for days
Out of the Institut’s orbit come blue-haired ideologues and, far more dangerous, the sleeper agents: some 80 senior civil servants calling themselves the Phrygians, formed in May this year. They meet each month, co-ordinate by Telegram, and embed themselves at the finance ministry, the foreign ministry, the Banque de France and the European Commission. Their handler is the beautiful Clémence Guetté, who co-chairs the Institut with Mélenchon and runs the programme.
No other political family or faction in modern France is as well organised as LFI. This is one hell of a tight ship. I would willingly grant that their presidential prospects are poor for this cycle. But I would not be so bold as to dismiss their chances entirely.
LFI has something no other party seems able to hold on to: a disciplined strategy for attaining and keeping power. They have bet everything on Islam and its representatives, abandoning the workers of old in favour of immigrants and their descendants.
Sixty-nine per cent of French Muslims voted for Mélenchon in the first round of 2022. It is a bloc more cohesive than any other group voting for anyone, anywhere (he scored 88 per cent in some areas). If demographic curves are to be believed – which they are – this is bound to be a winning strategy, if not next year, then soon.
But Mélenchon would also be wise not to trust in his own invincibility. He may yet be consumed by his new friends, who have proven, on more than one occasion, perfectly willing to devour their own.

articles.title_orig: Meta Offers Zuckerberg New Shares to Keep Him in California
articles.title_zh: Meta Offers Zuckerberg New Shares to Keep Him in California
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg enters the debate on AI regulation, arguing against slowing down development. National Review columnist Caroline Downey analyzes his stance on safety oversight and independent evaluators.
Mark Zuckerberg has reached an agreement with Meta to remain in California after raising the possibility of leaving the state amid concerns over a proposed billionaire wealth tax.
Zuckerberg, Meta's CEO , previously told the company he was considering moving his primary residence outside California because of Proposition 40, a ballot initiative that would impose a one-time tax equal to 5% of net worth on billionaires who were California residents on Jan. 1, 2026, if approved.
Under the agreement, Zuckerberg will receive non-voting shares that he could sell to help cover a potential wealth tax bill in exchange for a commitment to remain a resident of California , or the state where Meta maintains its headquarters, for eight years, according to Reuters.
Zuckerberg, the world's sixth-richest person with a net worth approaching $250 billion, according to Forbes, could face a substantial tax bill that might require him to sell company shares.
MARK RUFFALO CALLS GAVIN NEWSOM'S BILLIONAIRE TAX STANCE 'DISQUALIFYING' AHEAD OF CALIFORNIA VOTE
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reached an agreement with the company that could allow him to cover a potential California billionaire wealth tax bill while maintaining voting control, according to Reuters. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images / Getty Images)
If passed by voters in November, the tax would be due in 2027, although payments could be spread over five years at an additional cost. Real estate, pensions and retirement accounts generally would be excluded from the tax.
Zuckerberg can immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives, representing 10% of his overall economic stake in the company, potentially allowing him to pay the tax without giving up voting control, according to Reuters.
Meta said Wednesday that it planned to issue a new class of non-voting Class C common stock in January 2027 to help fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining Zuckerberg's control of the company.
In a statement provided to FOX Business, Meta pointed to comments from Chief Financial Officer Susan Li, who said the new shares were designed to help the company raise capital, compensate employees and pursue acquisitions while preserving its existing voting structure.
REAGAN ECONOMIST WARNS BILLIONAIRE TAX WOULD â€˜DESTROYâ€™ CALIFORNIA
Supporters hold signs advocating for the Billionaire Tax Now coalition during a news conference in Los Angeles, California, on Monday, April 27, 2026. (Caroline Brehman/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"We created this new class of shares with the purpose of creating a publicly traded non-voting stock usable for capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes while preserving the voting power of existing Class A and B shareholders," Li said during Meta's third-quarter earnings call.
Meta also said the decision followed a unanimous recommendation from a special committee of independent directors, which concluded that the new stock class would help finance the company's growth and preserve Zuckerberg's leadership.
According to a company filing, the committee emphasized the importance of Zuckerberg remaining in California to maintain close coordination with Meta's management and proximity to its Superintelligence Labs.
Although the ballot measure has been endorsed by the California Democratic Party, some prominent Democrats, including Gov. Gavin Newsom , have opposed it.
Economist Art Laffer, a former economic adviser to President Ronald Reagan, previously warned that the measure could accelerate an exodus of California's wealthiest residents.
META ORDERED TO PAY $25B AFTER JURY FINDS IT MISLED USERS ON DATA PRIVACY
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg could sell newly issued non-voting shares to help cover a potential tax bill if California voters approve a proposed billionaire wealth tax. (David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"No one would want to go there to build their wealth only to be faced with this type of tax. It would cause an exodus of billionaires, which have not left California because the income taxes do not affect the billionaires much at all. This tax would really affect them," Laffer said.
California entrepreneur Eric Schiffer, chairman of the family office Patriarch and CEO of Reputation Management Consultants, previously told FOX Business that passage of the measure could prompt wealthy entrepreneurs to leave California.
"I think the impact of this passing in California is a giant sucking sound of all of these entrepreneurs being sucked out of California because they're just not going to want to stay," Schiffer said.
California's nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office (LAO) said "some billionaires" may decide to leave the state in response to the tax, potentially reducing the income tax revenue they generate.
The LAO also estimated that departures and other behavioral changes could reduce state income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually. However, the office estimated that the wealth tax could generate tens of billions of dollars over several years.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: U.S. reduces troop footprint in Mideast as indirect talks with Iran continue
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: U.S. reduces troop footprint in Mideast as indirect talks with Iran continue
articles.content_orig:
Top European diplomats will hold talks in Istanbul Friday with their counterparts from Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt during a meeting initiated by Ankara, a Turkish foreign ministry source told the AFP news agency on Thursday.
Foreign ministers from the so-called E3 group – Britain, France and Germany – will meet counterparts from the newly created R4 group to discuss the Palestinian issue, developments in Yemen and the Strait of Hormuz and ways to end the Russia-Ukraine war, the source said.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan will host the meeting, the first to bring together the two groups.
"The seven countries will come together for the first time in the R4+E3 format, at Turkey's initiative," the source said, indicating they would explore "opportunities for cooperation and coordination that could be put into practice ... in the coming period."
In chairing the meeting, Fidan was expected to focus on the international community "increasing pressure on Israel" in response to its settlement expansion and its "encouragement of settler terrorism," the source AFP.
Fidan will also underline support for Saudi Arabia's security in the face of attacks by Yemen's Houthis, and stress the need for permanent freedom of navigation in the Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Straits.
Saudi Arabia's state-owned Saudi Aramco, the world's biggest oil company, told staff to evacuate the company's headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran and to work remotely, the Reuters news agency reported Thursday, citing six sources with knowledge of the matter.
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels have hit the kingdom repeatedly with missile and drone attacks in recent weeks.
Last week a missile struck an Aramco building in Dhahran, which is on Saudi Arabia's Persian Gulf coast. The strike caused a "limited fire" at Saudi Aramco's headquarters complex, the kingdom's energy ministry said at the time.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen's escalating civil war said Thursday that it had intercepted another drone over the Saudi capital Riyadh.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki confirmed the interception in a social media post, without offering further details.
Saudi Arabia has been pummeled by Houthi strikes in recent weeks. Experts say geography, missile interceptor shortages and evolving Houthi tactics are helping the Iranian proxy menace the kingdom, and global energy supplies .
World shares and U.S. futures retreated Thursday as oil prices jumped more than 2% following a report by Iran's state television that seven oil tankers were hit by its military or sea mines and damaged near the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
If the claim by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps is verified, it would be the largest number of vessels damaged in the Gulf in a single day since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28.
Brent crude, the international standard, gained 3.2% to hit $112.27 per barrel Thursday. It has been bouncing around $110 in recent days amid uncertainty about when the war with Iran might ease to allow the global energy shipments through the Strait of Hormuz to return to normal.
U.S. benchmark crude rose 2.8% to $99.80 per barrel.
In early European trading, Germany's DAX shed 1.1% to 25,367.96, while the CAC 40 in Paris declined 1.3% to 7,816.67. Britain's FTSE 100 was down 0.7% at 10,678.67.
The future for the S&P 500 lost 1% and that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was 0.7% lower.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Thursday that it had struck four vessels transferring oil ship-to-ship in the Persian Gulf after they used a route through the Strait of Hormuz that Iran rejects. Ship-to-ship cargo transfers have become more common as tankers and other commercial vessels try to avoid Iranian detection and strikes in the strategic waterway.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy said it "monitored and pursued four violating vessels that had previously passed through an illegal route," referring to shipping lanes in the strait that the Trump administration has encouraged vessels to use to avoid Iranian fees and controls. Tehran considers those southern routes, close to Oman's coast, unauthorized and has targeted vessels trying to use them for months.
"They discovered the vessels transferring oil cargoes from ship to ship in the north-central part of the Persian Gulf," the bulletin read. "All four ships were hit simultaneously and are burning."
The IRGC said three other ships attempting to use routes not recognized by Iran "suffered accidents and caught fire after striking mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, and were brought to a halt."
The IRGC said the U.S. "encouraging vessels to pass through an illegally mined passage has led to an increasing number of maritime incidents day by day."
"If this course continues," the group warned, "the confrontation will extend to the bases of the aggressors in the region."
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said Thursday that the latest attack on the kingdom's airports, a strike on the eastern city of Dammam's King Fahd International Airport, had risen to two.
"The number of deaths resulting from the attack has risen to two, after confirming an additional death. The deceased were a Saudi citizen and a resident of Indian nationality," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement shared on social media.
It said eight others, "a Saudi citizen, two residents each of Indian, Yemeni, and Bangladeshi nationalities, and a resident of Nepalese nationality," were injured in the attack.
The statement did not assign blame for the attack, but Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have attacked Saudi airports and other infrastructure for weeks in retaliation for the Saudi government's backing of Yemeni state forces in the neighboring nation's decade-long civil war.
GACA said in its statement that it was continuing work in conjunction with other security authorities "to assess the damages, and to take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and employees, and to maintain the security and safety of the civil aviation system in the Kingdom."
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent weeks have inflicted severe losses on the kingdom and prompted the U.S. to quietly reduce its military footprint in the region as missiles hit energy infrastructure and civilian airports, killing more than 20 people.
Saudi Arabia, despite its size, wealth and a substantial military, has appeared to be on the back foot as it faces the Yemeni rebels.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute — far more than any other country in the Middle East , including Israel.
So, why has the kingdom struggled to stop the Houthi barrage? Read our full story here .
An attack targeting the King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed one person and injured eight others Wednesday evening, the kingdom's civil aviation authority said.
The authority said in a statement that injuries from the attack ranged from "minor to serious" and that material damage to the airport was also being assessed.
It did not describe what type of attack occurred, but the kingdom's airports have been targeted repeatedly by projectiles in recent days by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi militants.
A U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday the military has been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran.
NBC News was first to report on the drawdowns.
Asked about the reports, U.S. Central Command spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins told CBS News: "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."

articles.title_orig: Toyota recalls over 105,000 vehicles. See the affected model
articles.title_zh: Toyota recalls over 105,000 vehicles. See the affected model
articles.content_orig:
Toyota has issued a rather strange recall for the 2024-2027 Land Cruiser . It also seems rather comprehensive; the recall population numbers 105,794, which is nearabout the total number of Land Cruisers sold in the U.S. so far for the current J250 generation.
The issue stems from a retaining clip that connects fuel tubes from the gas tank to the engine. Specifically, there’s a resin fuel tube on the tank that connects to a main metal fuel tube, the latter of which delivers gas to the engine. Toyota says that if the retaining clip on the connector between the two is lifted, there’s a possibility of a fuel leak—and of course, a fuel leak means an increased chance of fire.
Toyota conducted a years-long investigation into this issue, starting all the way back in July 2024. You can read the full timeline of events here , but we’ll summarize the six-page document for you.
Toyota became aware of the issue when field reports noted the retainer clip holding the fuel tubes together was lifted or missing. How this happened was vigorously investigated, but Toyota found no issues in the part or its manufacturing processes. One theory suggested in the report is that some recovered connectors showed evidence of markings that could’ve been caused by someone disconnecting the tubes after manufacturing. Additionally, other markings seen on certain clips were consistent with prior supplier testing.
When it comes to the fire risk, Toyota says it evaluated the temperatures of nearby components, finding all of them below the ignition temperature of fuel.
The most recent testing from Toyota this year attempted to identify how the retainer clip at this connection could become lifted. None of the tests provided the information Toyota was looking for; that said, among 400 field vehicles where no connector disconnects had been alleged / leaks reported, Toyota identified one with a lifted retainer clip. Despite the clip being lifted, that one vehicle was not leaking fuel.
Toyota ultimately decided to conduct this recall based on its fuel leak volume evaluation, and the number of field cases it observed of the clip being lifted. As of this recall, Toyota is aware of 23 field reports and 64 warranty claims that relate to the issue. With the cause and circumstances around how the issue manifests, Toyota is unsure what percentage of vehicles might contain this defect.
The fix is relatively simple. Dealers will inspect the connection and install a supplemental clamp. If necessary, they’ll replace the resin fuel tube, too. Notifications to owners are expected to occur by December 13 this year, and per federal law , all recall work will be completed free of charge.

articles.title_zh: France’s Debt Crisis Deepens as Foreign Investors Look for the Exit
articles.content_orig:
France’s bond market hit by another bout of selling as country recovers from weekend protests
Business live – latest updates
French borrowing costs continued to rise on Thursday, as investors fret that France’s government is struggling to pass a federal budget after public protests gripped the country.
France’s bond market was hit with another bout of selling, with the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs – a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – rising to its highest level in almost 15 years.
The yield on the French 10-year bond – known as obligation assimilables du Trésor ( Oat ) – rose by nine basis points to 5.089% in early trading on Thursday, its highest level since July 2022. It broke across the 5% threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002.
The move lifted France’s 10-year borrowing costs over the equivalent for US Treasury bonds for the first time since 2013.
The volatility comes as the French government struggles to pass a budget for next year, while the country recovers from widespread protests that turned violent last weekend.
Tens of thousands of people had attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille in recent days.
Public buildings were attacked, and thousands of shops and businesses were looted. The interior ministry said there had been nearly 2,400 arrests.
Meanwhile, a parliamentary gridlock has blocked plans by the president, Emmanuel Macron, to increase the state pension age from 62 to 64 and a series of measures designed to rein in state spending.
France’s budget deficit was 5.1% of gross domestic product in 2025, while its debt pile stood at 115.6% of GDP.
It comes as the country also grapples with higher inflation triggered by the war in Iran, with many governments with big debt piles coming under acute pressure.
Jim Reid, a market strategist at Deutsche Bank, said the sell-off in French government bonds was starting to ripple out to other countries, too.

“Among others, the Italian 10-year spread over [German bonds] widened 3.8 basis points to 116 basis points, while Spain’s widened 3.1 basis points to 66 basis points, marking its widest level since June 2025,” he said.
Carsten Brzeski of the bank ING said rising yields had reinforced the European Central Bank’s “restrictive” monetary policy stance before its interest rate decision next week. The bank last raised its key interest rate to 2.5% in September .
“The ECB is very likely to stay on hold next week and will delay any next rate hike decision to December,” he said.
“Any solution to the current French fiscal woes could bring some relief to bond markets and allow the ECB to continue hiking rates. Without any solution, bond markets have taken over the ECB’s role, making rate hikes less likely.”

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Met Xi Jinping and Took Tesla FSD to China — Now His CFO Says Getting the Green Light for Unsup
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Met Xi Jinping and Took Tesla FSD to China — Now His CFO Says Getting the Green Light for Unsup
articles.content_orig:
The logo of Tesla is displayed on a smartphone screen with the SpaceX logo in the background.
The world’s richest man has publicly backed a potential combination of SpaceX and Tesla in what could be the biggest merger in history.
On Tuesday, Elon Musk , the CEO and largest shareholder of both companies, said the electric vehicle maker and the rocket company had formed special committees at the request of shareholders to discuss the idea.
“I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity, ​and there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating,” Musk told SpaceX investors on a conference call.
“I think it would be a good ​idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies,” he added.
The committees, which are made up of independent directors, would need to agree on the transaction terms of any deal before putting it to shareholders for a vote. Musk said his conflict of interest prevents him from participating in their discussions.
Musk has previously teased a Tesla-SpaceX merger. On a July 22 earnings call, Musk said there was “more and more overlap” between Tesla and SpaceX as the companies expand into artificial intelligence and robotics. Last week, Barclays analysts suggested that a merger could be announced before Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting in December.
Tuesday’s call was the first confirmation that the companies were formally exploring a combination.
A merger could create a company worth around $3.5 trillion , putting it among the world’s most valuable companies. It could also become the biggest merger ever by deal value, potentially surpassing SpaceX’s record-setting $250 billion acquisition of Musk-owned AI company xAI in February. SpaceX is currently valued at about $2 trillion, and Tesla at $1.5 trillion. A deal could also help propel Musk back into trillionaire ranks , depending on its terms and how investors value the combined company. Musk owns around 48% of SpaceX and 20% of Tesla.
The shares of both companies rose in after-hours trading on Tuesday. SpaceX, which went public in June, reported a quarterly net profit of $4.4 billion. Musk told investors he expects annual recurring revenue of between $500 billion and $1 trillion by the end of 2027.
Some analysts, however, have warned of regulatory and geopolitical hurdles, particularly in terms of Tesla’s Chinese operations and SpaceX’s U.S. defence work. Morningstar analysts said a merger could raise U.S. national security concerns involving the combined company’s supply chain. JPMorgan analysts also flagged regulatory approval in China as a potential stumbling block.
Any deal could also face congressional scrutiny, which could intensify if Democrats win control of either chamber in the coming midterm elections. Democratic lawmakers have previously questioned Musk over conflicts of interest and raised national security concerns about reported Chinese investments in SpaceX. Democrats have also challenged major acquisitions in the past on consumer protection grounds. In June, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D, Mass.) criticized SpaceX’s IPO, citing Musk’s concentrated voting power and weak investor protections—concerns that could resurface in a Tesla-SpaceX merger.
A merger could bring two of Musk’s biggest businesses under one corporate umbrella, making it easier for the companies to move investments and resources between projects. “This would allow him to run all their operations under one roof without tripping on as many governance issues,” wrote Morningstar analysts Seth Goldstein and Nicolas Owens in June. “For example, Musk could move Tesla software developers or engineers to work on SpaceX AI projects, and vice versa, or have Tesla and SpaceX supply one another without the need for related party transaction disclosures or risking shareholder lawsuits claiming the resources of one firm are being diverted for the benefit of the other.”
Analysts noted that Tesla’s robotaxis could benefit from Starlink connectivity, while its autonomous vehicles and Optimus humanoid robots could more closely integrate SpaceX’s AI technology. SpaceX’s planned orbital data centers, meanwhile, could potentially benefit from access to Tesla’s battery and energy storage products.
A combined company could also mean greater control of several stages of the AI value chain, from chip design and planned manufacturing to computing infrastructure, AI software, and its deployment in vehicles and robots.
The companies already collaborate. In March, they announced Terafab , a joint semiconductor manufacturing project intended to produce chips for Tesla’s vehicles and humanoid robots and SpaceX’s planned AI satellites. SpaceX technologies have also been used in some Tesla products, including the new Roadster prototype , which uses SpaceX-developed thrusters.
David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group, told the BBC that a merger also appears to align with Musk’s long-held ambition of colonizing Mars . Musk previously outlined plans to send Tesla’s Optimus robots to the planet aboard SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft.
A merger could also strengthen Musk’s influence over Tesla’s direction. Barclays estimated that a SpaceX acquisition of Tesla could give Musk around 37% of the combined company while controlling around 56% of its voting power. He currently controls around 82% of voting power at SpaceX and 20% at Tesla . That could represent either a benefit or a risk for shareholders, as decision-making would become faster but have fewer checks.
“One thing I don’t think people talk enough about with SpaceX and Tesla as well: You do still have a huge amount of key-man risk here,” wrote Morningstar analyst David Sekera earlier this month. “God forbid anything were to happen to Elon Musk.”

When it rains space debris.

The rocket was developed by LandSpace, a Chinese commercial space startup and departed from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China on October 14, 2026, carrying ten satellites.
Minnesota object. Image credit: Stevens County Sheriff’s Office
Yet another incident of possible space junk took place on October 14, 2026, at approximately 3:30pm, the Stevens County Sheriff’s Office in Minnesota received a phone call of foreign debris that was found in a cornfield in Scott Township.
“Upon responding, deputies confirmed that a large, metallic object, approximately 11-feet in diameter, presumably a space object, was present in the cornfield,” reports the sheriff’s office.
The Minnesota duty officer was notified of this and federal agencies responded.
“The Sheriff’s Office is working closely with several state and federal agencies to identify and notify the owner of the debris and to plan for removal from the field. Agency officials have determined that there is no danger to the public due to this incident,” the office stated in a press release.

In both cases – Sampit and Scott Township — the recovered fragments are being examined to help identify their origin.

articles.title_orig: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
articles.title_zh: 5 simple ways to relieve the aches and pains of sitting at a desk all day
articles.content_orig:
Back pain, eye strain, sluggishness, shoulder aches, restlessness.
If you sit in front of a computer for long periods of time, whether it's for work or leisure, you've probably experienced one of these symptoms.
But there are ways to relieve some of this discomfort — and even combat some of the health risks that may come with prolonged sitting. That includes walking breaks, ergonomic solutions and quick, simple stretches.
Here's a roundup of tips that have been previously featured on Life Kit.
We know that a sedentary lifestyle isn't great for human health. Studies have shown it can lead to fatigue, weight gain and back and joint pain — and it's been linked to chronic diseases like obesity, heart disease and cancer. Yet adults in the United States spend an average of 9.5 hours sitting per day, involved in activities tied to computers, laptops and phones.
But there may be a way to mitigate its harms. In 2023, researchers at Columbia University Medical Center set out to find the least amount of movement you need to counteract the dangers of prolonged sitting. And they found that walking for five minutes every 30 minutes was the most effective strategy .
In 2023, our colleagues at NPR's Body Electric tested out this five-minute walking exercise on our NPR listeners. Over 20,000 participants joined the challenge — and reported higher productivity and lower fatigue .
Want to give this walking challenge a try? Get instructions from Body Electric — and use this worksheet to keep track of your walking breaks .
Anyone who works at a desk knows how easy it can be to slip into a slouch. If we're not careful, that mid-back rounding can creep into all of our sitting time and create pain by putting stress on the middle section of our spine.
This movement above seeks to relieve that stress and encourage flexibility by mimicking the natural movements of the spine — side bending, bending backward and rotating, says Vinh Pham, a physical therapist. The idea is to get the body comfortable with these motions so that when you encounter them in real life, they're not painful.
To do this modified movement, which Pham calls the 3D T-spine rotation, stand up and drop your right foot behind the left, about a foot apart. Starting with the right arm straight up and the left arm behind you, as if you're shaking the hand of the person behind you, simultaneously drop your arms — still in a straight position — and twist toward your right foot. Move them back to their original position and hold for two seconds. Repeat the movement ten times before switching legs and doing the same exercise on the other side.
For more pain-relieving stretches, read this story.
When you stare at a screen for long periods of time, your eyes have to work hard. They must first turn inward to look at a close subject, then adjust the focus for short vision and hold that position.
Digital eye strain, as eye doctors call it, can cause eye fatigue, headaches or blurry vision. Try the exercise below to relieve that strain.
Fidgeting is a sign you need to break out of a stagnant posture, says Katy Bowman , a biomechanist and author of Rethink Your Position and Movement Matters . Even a position that feels comfortable at first can begin causing back pain, headaches or stiffness if you hold it long enough .
So listen to your body and mix things up. Alternate between sitting, standing, reclining and moving. That might mean opting to stand in the back of a conference room during a big staff meeting, taking a call while going on a walk or reading a report with your feet propped up in the break room.
The goal is to put yourself in configurations that contort your body in different ways. They should be "adaptive and dynamic" and easy to "change in and out of," says Leada Malek , a physical therapist and author of the book Science of Stretch.
Don't worry too much about what is "good" and "bad" posture. Both Malek and Bowman agree on a common phrase among physical therapists: "Your best posture is your next posture."
Your monitor screen should be at eye level so you're not craning your head down to see. And, your keyboard and mouse should be low enough so you're not shrugging your shoulders and lifting up your arms like a praying mantis to type and click.
Meg Honan, a professional ergonomist, says this common "head down and arms up" position sets you up to feel "achy, sore and tired." To combat this uncomfortable and oftentimes painful position, try repositioning your tech. Bring your laptop or desktop monitor screen up to eye level with a stack of books or some other platform.
Place your keyboard and mouse at a lower height where you don't have to shrug your shoulders to use them. If your keyboard is attached to your laptop, consider connecting an external keyboard and mouse so you can have the computer screen at your eye level and lower your arms. External mouses don't just help lower our arms, but they also prevent the constant strain of using a trackpad.
For more ergonomic tips, read our story .

articles.title_orig: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
articles.title_zh: How long does it take to save up for a starter home? Twice as long as it did in 2019
articles.content_orig:
For-sale signs are posted in front of condominiums for sale in July in Los Angeles. A new analysis from the Center for Responsible Lending finds that the average renter household now needs 16 years to save for a down payment and closing costs. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption
Mortgage rates topping 7% is the latest sign of how hard it has gotten to buy a first house, with aspiring owners already facing sky-high prices. A new analysis out Thursday shines a light on yet another growing obstacle: the amount needed to close a home loan.
"Over the last seven years, the time to save up that down payment and closing costs has doubled," said Mike Calhoun, president of the Center for Responsible Lending, a research nonprofit that promotes economic opportunity. The report was released by the center's Julian Bond Institute .
Since 2019, the last time the center made the same calculation, home prices have shot up, inflation spiked and has remained stubbornly high, and the rising cost of food, gas, healthcare and more has strained family budgets. Closing costs on a home loan have also ticked up, driven in part by rising homeowners insurance.
Amid all this, renters' incomes have not kept pace, and personal savings rates have dropped.
Today, the center calculates that for a median-income renter household, it would take a "staggering 16 years" to save up a down payment and closing costs for a starter home. That's twice as long as in 2019. And it would take even more time — 21 years — for a median-income Black renter household.
That kind of time frame upends a main reason that many look to buy in the first place. As the analysis notes, "young children at the time the family starts saving may have left the household — for higher education or the workforce — before the family will have saved enough to purchase their first home."
The report also narrows its calculations to middle-income households — making roughly $50,000 to $120,000 — whose members are more likely to be viable homeowners. For them, the savings time has also doubled, to 12 years.
For front-line workers, such as police officers, firefighters, EMTs, nurses and teachers, the researchers find that "the years to save has at least doubled and now ranges from 10 to 13 years."
As stark as those numbers are, Calhoun said they're likely an undercount.
The center's calculations are for a 3.5% down payment, since that's what the Federal Housing Administration requires for first-time buyers. The median first-time buyer actually puts down about 10% . The report also assumes families are really "stretching their savings," he said, even though many can't save at all, are forced to eat into savings or take on debt.
The Center for Responsible Lending's report highlights a sharp divide in the housing economy, exacerbated when the COVID-19 pandemic triggered a spike in inflation, mortgage rates and home prices.
"If you look at the last seven years, they have been extraordinarily good to homeowners," Calhoun said. Those who bought when prices were far lower have accumulated enormous equity as home values have shot up. Some were also able to lower their monthly payments by refinancing, as mortgage rates hit historic lows of around 2% or 3% before they spiked.
Many homeowners with low rates have decided they can't afford to move and see their mortgage payments double. That has meant fewer older adults downsizing and fewer overall putting their homes on the market, intensifying a national housing shortage.
Meanwhile, rising rents have consumed an increasing share of family incomes, according to a recent report by the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies. "From 2001 to 2024, renter incomes rose by 9 percent in real terms while rents rose by 30 percent," it says. This has left a quarter of renters paying more than half their income on rent and utilities.
Despite a recent softening in rental markets, a record number of renters are still considered cost burdened. Lower-income households are also hit harder by inflation, since basic goods and services make up a larger portion of their budgets.
The center calculates a starter home cost of $335,574, which is 80% of the median sales price of existing homes. And the center finds that it takes less time to save a down payment and closing costs for that in some major metropolitan areas than others — from 11 years in Houston to 24 in Los Angeles.
The report also notes that housing costs have outstripped incomes pretty much everywhere and that "the problem is even more acute in the fastest-growing rural areas than in urban areas." A recent analysis by center-left think tank Third Way found that housing construction has been unable to keep up with rural growth, creating severe pressure on affordability.
The widening housing wealth gap leaves a more privileged share of Americans who are able to buy a home. "Cash purchases are way up," Calhoun said. For younger buyers, "the overwhelming way people come up with the money is from assistance from family , the 'bank of mom and dad' and friends."
Far fewer buyers get help from down payment assistance programs, even though there are thousands of them. "The programs often run out of money," Calhoun said. "A lot of these are very small, idiosyncratic."
He'd like to see more assistance programs "to reach a broader array of people who don't have intergenerational wealth."
The center's report also calls for zoning and other reforms to boost the supply of smaller, cheaper starter homes, including duplexes, townhomes and manufactured housing. A sweeping new law passed by Congress this year aims to promote that, but the onus is on states and cities to follow up, and creating new supply will take time.
Despite all this, a related survey from the center finds that millennials and Gen Zers aspire to homeownership at the same rate as earlier generations — a "testament to the resilience of the American dream," according to Thursday's report.
It's the main way "most families generate wealth that they can pass on to the next generation," said report co-author David Silberman. "I think the case for homeownership remains really strong, despite all the trends we're pointing to in the challenges of getting there."

articles.title_orig: Minneapolis restaurant that offered free meals to protest ICE raids announces closure
articles.title_zh: Minneapolis restaurant that offered free meals to protest ICE raids announces closure
articles.content_orig:
Modern Times Café, a Minneapolis restaurant that attempted to eliminate prices, has announced it will be closing for good by the end of the year.
“For the last six years, I’ve been trying to prove that Modern Times can continue to exist,” owner Dylan Alverson wrote on social media Saturday. “I’ve exhausted every option without compromising the core fundamentals that make Modern Times what it is.”
He added that he plans to spend the next two months celebrating the 16-year-old business and discussing ways for a business like his to continue.
“The only way for places like Modern Times to exist in the future is to actively challenge the reasons why it can no longer exist,” Alverson wrote.
Alverson announced on Instagram in January that his business, which rebranded as Post Modern Times, would operate as a “free and donation-based restaurant” where everyone would be welcome “except ICE” in protest of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations happening in his state, partly in response to the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti.
“We absolutely cannot go on as we have. I am sick of generating money for the soldiers in our streets and for a government that won’t protect us — a government who is actively inflicting daily harm on its citizens,” Alverson wrote. “Effective tomorrow we are done making money for the fascists that occupy our city.”
The decision was made after Pretti was shot and killed by Border Patrol agents.
The Modern Times Café operated without prices for about six months until it briefly closed in July .
The establishment returned to using prices once the store reopened in August but announced that it would continue serving 25 free meals per day.
By October, Alverson told The New York Times he was operating under a “zero profit margin,” hoping that his place could be used as a model for other restaurants.
“If I can create a fundraising mechanism that can raise money to provide hospitality, we can take that program and add restaurants to it,” Alverson said.
However, he acknowledged that the process was taxing for his staff and led to customers waiting up to two hours for a meal, half of which would usually be given for free.
Neighbors also expressed concerns that homeless and drug-addicted people would take advantage of the offer.
In a comment to Fox News Digital, Alverson stood by his remarks to The New York Times and suggested that the bigger issue was other restaurants that were struggling.
“I think a bigger question right now is how many independent restaurants are close to collapse?” Alverson said.

articles.title_orig: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.title_zh: China's Stock Market Crashes 20%: 3 Reasons Why The Dragon Is Losing Its Fire
articles.content_orig:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.
The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.
Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.
"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.
Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.
The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.
Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.
Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.
"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.
Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

articles.title_orig: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence
articles.title_zh: World's largest wealth fund posts $30 billion loss after bond market turbulence
articles.content_orig:
Norway's sovereign wealth fund — the largest in the world — said Thursday that its investment portfolio delivered a loss of $30 billion in the third quarter, as rising interest rates dented returns on its bond holdings.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), which manages the $2.3 trillion fund, said the accounting return for the period was a loss of 278 billion kroner ($29.7 billion). Around 70% of NBIM's fixed income portfolio is allocated to government bonds, with the remainder invested in corporate debt.
The third quarter saw a global bond market rout . Government bond yields surged as major central banks, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, began rate-hiking cycles and concerns about inflation and government debt levels mounted.
NBIM's fixed income investments delivered a negative return of 3.5%, with the fund's management saying this was a key driver of the overall downturn.
"The fund's return was close to flat, ending slightly negative as rising interest rates led to weaker results on our fixed-income investments," NBIM's Deputy CEO Trond Grande said in a statement.
Fixed income accounts for just over a quarter of the fund's entire portfolio, with NBIM invested in 1,664 bonds across 51 countries.
Last month, NBIM said it wanted to cut its U.S. Treasury holdings as part of wider plans to reduce its allocation to government-issued debt.
Equities, which account for 72% of the sovereign wealth fund's investments, returned 0.5% for the fund in the third quarter.
The fund has small stakes in around 7,100 companies across most countries. With holdings in 1.5% of all listed companies globally, it is the world's largest single investor.
Stock markets were turbulent in the three months to September. Wall Street's major averages ended the third quarter in mixed territory. The S&P 500 index added 2.03%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ended the quarter 2.2% higher.
The average change across the three indexes was just 0.6%, marking a slowdown in the rally that saw double-digit gains in the previous quarter.
NBIM is an investor in America's biggest companies, with its top holdings including a $65.4 billion stake in Nvidia , as well as positions in Apple , Alphabet and Microsoft .
Its positions in the world's biggest companies make NBIM influential in terms of both voting power and setting investment trends.
"Equity returns were also close to zero, but there were large differences between sectors. Energy companies rose the most, while interest-rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate fell," Grande said Thursday.
Energy stocks benefited from surging oil prices in the third quarter, as the U.S.-Iran war continued, said NBIM, which has stakes in various energy majors, including Exxon Mobil , Shell and Chevron .
Over the summer, NBIM CEO Nicolai Tangen told CNBC that investors should not expect a continuation of the bumper gains seen in the stock market in the first half of this year.
"For sure, we should not be expecting the same kind of returns going forward as we've seen over the last six months," he said at the time.
The fund delivered a first-half return of 12.95%, and a record first-half profit nearing $185 billion. It also invests in real estate and renewable energy infrastructure, which returned 0.4% and 7.5%, respectively, in the third quarter.
Norway established its sovereign wealth fund in 1998 to invest revenues from the country's oil.

articles.title_orig: Australian Zoo Plays Matchmaker for Giant Birds, and Big Green Eggs Are Proof
articles.title_zh: Australian Zoo Plays Matchmaker for Giant Birds, and Big Green Eggs Are Proof
articles.content_orig:
Adelaide Zoo recorded its first Southern Cassowary egg in 34 years.
Ten-year-old Martina laid the bright green egg after being paired with 13-year-old Jeffrey.
The egg's fertility is unknown, and incubation takes about 50 days.
Adelaide Zoo in Australia celebrated the arrival of its first cassowary eggs in decades.
Two cassowary eggs were laid over the last few days, according to the zoo's Facebook page.
The milestone comes after caretakers carefully paired the zoo's female cassowary, 10-year-old Martina, with its 13-year-old male, Jeffrey, for the first time.
FILE - One of two cassowary eggs that were laid at Adelaide Zoo. (Zoos SA via Storyful)
Zoo employees have yet to confirm whether the eggs are even fertilized, but the fact that the eggs were laid at all is still a huge success for the species, according to a zoo news release.
"This is really exciting news for us because it has been 34 years since we've had successful cassowary chicks here at Adelaide Zoo, so the team and myself included are very excited," Team Supervisor Birds and Free Flight, Erin, said.
Since it is unclear whether the eggs have been fertilized, caretakers will be monitoring the nesting area and the birds' behavior closely in the meantime.
Cassowary can lay a clutch of between three and five eggs, according to the zoo.
It takes about 50 days to incubate and typically the male cassowary cares for and raises the chicks.
The bright green color of the shell helps camouflage the eggs from predators, according to the zoo.

articles.content_orig: WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Ranking Member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Roger Wicker (R-MS), Chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Chuck Grassley (R-IA), Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, Chris Murphy (D-CT), Joni Ernst (R-IA) and Thom Tillis (R-NC) released the following statement ahead of Serbia’s upcoming parliamentary elections on October 25, 2026, calling for Serbian authorities to ensure the elections are free and fair. The Senators’ statement comes as independent election monitors are raising concerns that the upcoming elections will take place in a hostile environment for civil society, observers and opposition parties. According to Serbia’s independent, non-partisan Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA) and the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe’s (OSCE) Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), the campaign period has seen several instances of voter intimidation, abuse of administrative resources to benefit the ruling party and intimidation of opposition candidates by police. CRTA noted that this campaign is “unlike any electoral process [it] has observed before” and identified cases of wiretapping of opposition candidates. These concerns are similar to shortcomings that were raised after the 2022 elections, which have still not been addressed by the ruling party. “As Serbians prepare to go to the polls on October 25, we stand for their right to make their voices heard in free and fair conditions and urge all parties to respect the vote count and relevant processes for verifying electoral results. The United States has long supported Serbia’s path to Euro-Atlantic integration and has acknowledged its potential to promote stability in the Western Balkans. Robust democracy in Serbia is essential for each of those goals. “Unfortunately, both Serbian and international election observers found serious infringements to the integrity of the previous parliamentary elections in 2022. We are now seeing similarly troubling signs ahead of the October 25 vote. Reports of unlawful wiretapping of opposition members and attempts to discredit and undermine election observation missions are deeply concerning, and Serbian authorities must ensure a level playing field for all parties and open access to the polls for all citizens. “We urge the ruling party and all relevant institutions to ensure the peaceful, free and open conduct of the upcoming vote. We reaffirm the vital role that international and domestic observers play in safeguarding trust in the electoral process. The onus is on Serbian authorities to ensure that all institutions respect the role of citizen observers, journalists and candidates for office.”

articles.title_orig: El Salvador’s Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers
articles.title_zh: El Salvador’s Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers
articles.content_orig:
El Salvador has initiated a military operation to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers abducted by gangs in Haiti, President Nayib Bukele announced in a post on X, without elaborating.
Bukele, known for his intense crackdown on gang violence in El Salvador, warned in Wednesday’s statement that a more forceful response was coming if the personnel were not released alive and well.
“Do not take our word for empty threats,” the president wrote, addressing the gangs allegedly responsible for holding the four men. “We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too.”
Gangs in Haiti opened fire on an armoured vehicle carrying the men three days earlier, in the first major attack since an international gang suppression force began operating in the violence-wracked Caribbean country last year.
The four men, aviation technicians with the United Nations-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), have been missing since they fled the burning vehicle in the Santo area of Croix-des-Bouquets, Port-au-Prince.
Haiti’s government issued a news release on Wednesday evening saying the release of the abducted soldiers was an “absolute priority”.
It was not immediately clear if Haitian authorities received any confirmation that the Salvadoran soldiers are alive.
The government said a meeting was held at the prime minister’s office “to assess the ongoing interventions and determine the necessary measures to strengthen operations, in close collaboration with the Gang Repression Force”.
A spokesperson for the GSF did not immediately respond to a message seeking details
The UN-backed force is still fighting gangs in the community where Sunday’s attack occurred, warning residents in the area to remain indoors.
No one has claimed responsibility for the attack on the Salvadoran troops, which comes as Haiti prepares for its first general election in more than a decade. It also showcases the power of the gangs that control an estimated 70 percent of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
El Salvador is among several countries – including Chad, Jamaica and Guatemala – to form part of the gang suppression force, with more than 2,000 troops on the ground in Haiti.
Gang violence has displaced nearly 1.5 million people in Haiti in recent years. More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured from January through mid-September this year, and more than 230 have been kidnapped, according to the UN.
The area where the armoured vehicle was targeted is controlled by gangs, including Chèn Méchan; Kraze Barye, led by Vitel’Homme Innocent; and 400 Mawozo, led by Lanmo Sanjou.
Both gang leaders have been sanctioned by the UN and the US.

articles.title_orig: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
articles.title_zh: Meta hit with $25 billion penalty for misleading Facebook users
articles.content_orig:
A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion after the company was found to have misled users about its privacy practices in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal .
The Wednesday ruling marks one of the largest-ever legal penalties for a tech giant — and just the latest court loss for Meta this year.
The company, then known as Facebook, disclosed in 2018 that the private information of as many as 87 million Facebook users was improperly obtained by political analytics firm Cambridge Analytica . The firm used that information to build profiles of American voters.
New Mexico sued Facebook in 2021, accusing it of mishandling state residents’ personal information and deceiving those users about its policies in connection with the incident.
A jury found in September that Meta had violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act more than 43 million times. State District Court Judge Francis Mathew criticized the company for what he described as a “coherent strategy designed to mislead the public” in his Wednesday penalty decision.
“Facebook’s misrepresentations about users’ control of their data were not isolated incidents, but rather a systematic pattern of deception at the core of Facebook’s business model,” Mathew wrote.
After Wednesday’s penalty decision, Meta said it will appeal the decision and has accused New Mexico’s attorney general of conflating privacy and speech issues.
Meta agrees to pay $725 million to settle lawsuit over Cambridge Analytica data leak
“This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta Chief Legal Officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”
Meta’s legal battles threaten to strain its business, though court penalties and settlements remain relatively small compared to the company’s earnings so far.
The company reported earnings for the quarter ended in September on Wednesday, including lower quarterly profits than Wall Street had expected. It attributed the miss to a charge from the $18 billion multistate settlement it agreed to in August to resolve claims that its platforms have addicted and harmed young people.
New Mexico was not a party to that settlement, which also resolved the participating states’ outstanding claims related to Cambridge Analytica.
Meta posted income from operations of nearly $13 billion during the quarter, compared to nearly $23 billion that it said it would have earned without the settlement.
Meta settles landmark state child harm claims for $18 billion and promises changes to its platforms
Meta CFO Susan Li said on a call with analysts following the earnings report that the company is monitoring “active legal and regulatory matters that could significantly impact our business and financial results,” including additional youth-related trials set for later this year and next.
Meta was also ordered to pay nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case earlier this year over claims that its platforms addicted and harmed young people. Meta, along with YouTube, also lost a case in March in Los Angeles brought by a young woman with similar addiction and harm claims. The companies plan to appeal.
Still, Meta’s business continues to grow at a strong clip thanks in large part to its investments in artificial intelligence. The company posted sales growth of 26% year-on-year to more than $64 billion in the quarter.
Meta’s stock ( META ) jumped more than 3% in after-hours trading following the report on Wednesday.
Meta launched its Muse AI personal assistant app in September. The app quickly rocketed to the top of app stores and has gained more than 10 million users, according to the company. It also launched its latest foundation model, Muse Wonder, last month.
The company said Wednesday that its AI investments are boosting its core advertising business “through stronger engagement, better recommendations, and more efficient monetization.” Its average price per ad, a key metric for the company, jumped 14% year-over-year in the September quarter.
Across the industry, tech companies face questions about their heavy spending on AI infrastructure. Meta’s capital expenditures during the quarter reached nearly $35 billion, up 80% from the year-ago quarter. And the company narrowed its full-year capital expenditure guidance to between $135 billion to $145 billion, the upper end of the range it had previously provided. Meta declined to provide spending guidance for next year.
But investors are signaling they’re willing to give Meta some leeway, given the success of Muse, said Jesse Cohen, senior analyst at Investing.com .
“The market has shifted from punishing Meta for spending to rewarding it for having a compelling product story,” Cohen wrote in emailed commentary.

The IRGC again warned the U.S. against the resumption of military action.
Talks between the U.S. and Iran have stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February.
The two sides have since exchanged strikes. The U.S. says it is enforcing a blockade preventing any Iranian ships from entering or leaving the country, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.
Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military and oil infrastructure facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy claimed on Thursday to have attacked four vessels in the Strait of Hormuz, accusing the ships of navigating an "illegal route" and "transferring oil cargoes from one ship to another."
The ships were hit while in the north-central part of the Persian Gulf, the IRGC Navy claimed, in a statement published by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
The IRGC Navy also reported that three vessels hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday night.
The U.S. military has recently been repositioning personnel at U.S. military bases in the Middle East, according to a source familiar with the matter.
The repositioning of forces is similar to what occurred quietly prior to the start of the war with Iran in February, according to the source.
Asked for comment to an NBC report about the reduction of military and diplomatic personnel in the region, CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said in a statement, "We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness. We do not discuss related movements for operational security reasons. U.S. forces remain vigilant and ready to protect American personnel and interests across the region."
Earlier Wednesday, the State Department ordered the departure of non-essential personnel and family members in Saudi Arabia -- a decision officials say is a direct response to the risk posed by the Houthis.
There have been much smaller posture adjustments at several other embassies in the Middle East — changes officials say are also linked to the Houthi threat and other matters not connected to any plan to resume combat against Iran that the president may be considering.
-ABC News' Luis Martinez and Shannon Kingston
At least one person was killed and eight others injured in an attack on the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Arabia, on Wednesday, according to the Saudi civil aviation authority.
The injuries ranged from minor to severe, the authority said.
"The attack also resulted in material damage, which is currently being assessed," the authority said in a statement.
Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander Brig. Gen. Yadollah Javani warned that Iran could target seven critical undersea internet cables passing through the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. resumes attacks on Iran.
"The Americans and their allies possess significant assets; should they seek to damage our infrastructure, it is only natural that the Islamic Republic would leverage its full capabilities to readily destroy their assets and holdings, including the seven critical internet cables that run underwater through the Strait of Hormuz," Javani said in an interview with the state-run Al-Alam News Agency.
-ABC News' Charlotte Gardiner and Somayeh Malekian

articles.title_orig: Canada unveils $6.2bn plan to shield manufacturers as US tariffs bite
articles.title_zh: Canada unveils $6.2bn plan to shield manufacturers as US tariffs bite
articles.content_orig:
Canada has announced a $6.2 billion (€5.7 billion) package to protect its steel and auto industries from US tariffs, as Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that Washington has permanently altered a trade relationship built over decades.
Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford jointly unveiled the plan on Wednesday, directing $3.7 billion (€3.4 billion) to steelmakers and $1.8 billion (€1.65 billion) to automakers over five years, with $1.1 billion (€1 billion) of the auto funding coming from the federal government in Ottawa.
The announcement came the same day US-owned Cleveland-Cliffs confirmed layoffs at its Hamilton, Ontario, plant, underlining the human cost of the trade dispute.
“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage.”
The damage to the auto sector is already visible in the trade figures, as Canadian auto exports to the US have fallen more than 10 percent, while US exports to Canada have dropped more than 20 percent, a decline Carney said hurts both sides of the border.
“Tariffs make both our industries weaker and reduce choice for our families,” he stressed.
Carney confirmed he spoke at length with President Trump on Wednesday, covering trade, Iran and the Middle East.
He signalled no breakthrough but said Canada remains ready to negotiate. Talks collapsed in August after Trump imposed 50% tariffs on around $20 billion (€18.4 billion) in Canadian goods, prompting Canadian retaliation.
For his part, Ford was direct about what the dispute has done to bilateral ties. “No matter what happens in the midterms, no matter who sits in the White House, we’re not going back to the way things were,” he said.
Carney has set a target of doubling Canadian exports to non-US markets within a decade, acknowledging that an integrated North American auto industry may no longer be Washington’s priority.
“Their approach has changed,” he said. “So must ours.”
Meanwhile, the day took a sharper diplomatic turn when the US Embassy issued a statement accusing Canadian politicians of seeking to influence next month’s American midterm elections.
The embassy named Industry Minister Mélanie Joly for discussing retaliatory tariffs targeting Republican states and Ford for running a US television ad featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticising tariffs, the ad that prompted Trump to walk away from trade talks in October 2025.
Both leaders rejected the allegations. So did independent analysts.
“The implicit assumption that Canada could significantly alter the outcome of the midterms is absurd,” said Daniel Béland, political science professor at McGill University.
